title: London, Ontario Husband Charged With Second-Degree Murder in Death of Indian-Origin Mother of Two
excerpt: Raman Devi died September 15 after suffering critical injuries at her Chelton Road home; her husband Mandeep Singh, 41, has been charged and police are investigating the death as a femicide.
body:
• Raman Devi, a woman in her 30s and a mother of two, died on September 15 after suffering life-threatening injuries at her home on Chelton Road in London, Ontario.
  • Her husband, 41-year-old Mandeep Singh, has been charged with second-degree murder; police are investigating the case as a femicide tied to intimate partner violence.
  • Devi was five months away from completing a registered massage therapy programme she had pursued while raising a four-year-old son and a seven-year-old daughter.
  • If you or someone you know is experiencing intimate partner violence in Canada, call or text 1-866-863-0511 (Assaulted Women's Helpline) or find local supports at sheltersafe.ca.

London, Ontario police have charged a 41-year-old man with second-degree murder in the death of his wife, an Indian-origin woman in her 30s who died in hospital after officers found her with life-threatening injuries at the couple's home last month.

What happened

Police identified the woman as Raman Devi and said the incident occurred on September 15 at a residence on Chelton Road in the city's Summerside neighbourhood. Officers responding to the home found Devi critically injured; she was transported to hospital, where she later died, according to police and Canadian media reports.

Her husband, Mandeep Singh, 41, was charged with second-degree murder. Other family members were inside the home at the time, but no one else was injured. Singh appeared before a court on September 18 from the Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre, where he requested the assistance of a Punjabi interpreter during the proceedings.

A mother five months from a new career

Devi was raising two young children — a four-year-old son and a seven-year-old daughter — while completing a registered massage therapy programme. She was about five months away from finishing her studies and had been looking forward to beginning her professional career, according to friends and neighbours.

Her mother had travelled from India to help care for the children. Neighbour Sandra Sanchez, who launched a GoFundMe fundraiser to support Devi's mother and children, described her as a loving mother whose children were her world: "She was incredible, kind hearted, humble, caring, and always willing to help others." The Gurdwara London Sikh Society also set up a fundraiser for the family.

Investigating a femicide

London police have described the killing as a femicide resulting from intimate partner violence, and investigators are examining the history of the couple's relationship. The case comes after recent changes to Canada's Criminal Code concerning killings of women in the context of intimate-partner violence and coercive or controlling conduct; despite those changes, Singh is currently facing a second-degree murder charge, according to the National Times.

The death fits a troubling pattern. In July, 23-year-old Damanpreet Kaur died in Edmonton after being strangled; her partner was charged with second-degree murder in what police called an intimate partner homicide. Local advocates for survivors of gender-based violence say intimate-partner violence cuts across communities and urge neighbours to watch for warning signs and support people who may be afraid to seek help.

What's next

Singh remains in custody as the case proceeds through the Ontario court system. For the Indian diaspora in Canada, the tragedy is a stark reminder that support networks — from the Assaulted Women's Helpline at 1-866-863-0511 to community gurdwaras and settlement services — exist for families navigating domestic violence, and that asking for help early can save lives.
nri_angle: The death of Raman Devi — whose mother had travelled from India to help raise her grandchildren — underscores the vulnerability of immigrant families in Canada and the community support systems, from gurdwaras to helplines, that surround them.
author: Diaspora Desk
